hints: Think about what happens to hydrogen and electrons during respiration - they are removed from glucose and passed along, so what general type of chemistry does DCPIP take part in when it accepts them?
walkthrough:
Link DCPIP to respiration chemistry**
Respiration is essentially a series of oxidation and reduction reactions. Glucose is oxidised as hydrogen is removed from it, and other molecules are reduced as they gain that hydrogen.

Classify DCPIP**
DCPIP acts as an artificial hydrogen acceptor. It is reduced when it gains hydrogen from the respiring yeast and oxidised when it loses it, so it belongs to the redox group of indicators.

hints: Remember DCPIP starts in its oxidised state in the test-tube, then yeast respiration releases hydrogen that reduces it - focus on how the visible appearance differs between oxidised and reduced forms.
walkthrough:
Start and end states**
When first added, DCPIP is oxidised and appears blue. As yeast respires, it releases hydrogen from glucose oxidation.

Reduction causes loss of colour**
The hydrogen reduces DCPIP to its reduced form, which is colourless. So the observed change is blue to colourless, and faster decolourisation means faster respiration.

hints: Start by listing what is changing and what is being timed - temperature is the only factor allowed to vary, and time to decolourise is the result, so everything else added to the tube must be fixed.
Think about the three solutions mixed in each tube - the living cells, the food for respiration, and the dye itself - what aspects of amount could change the speed of colour loss if not controlled?
walkthrough:
Identify the fair-test logic**
Here temperature is the independent variable and time taken for DCPIP to change colour is the dependent variable. Any other factor that affects respiration rate or colour intensity must be kept constant.

Apply to the mixtures**
Keep the amount of yeast the same (volume / mass / concentration of suspension) so the number of respiring cells is equal. Keep the amount of substrate the same (volume / mass / concentration of glucose solution) and keep the amount of indicator the same (volume / concentration of DCPIP). Other valid controls include pH or equilibration time in the water-bath before adding DCPIP.

Final answer: Any two from: volume / mass / concentration of yeast suspension; volume / mass / concentration of glucose solution; volume / concentration of DCPIP; e.g. pH, time of equilibration before adding DCPIP.

hints: Look carefully at the y-axis in Fig. 6.1 - it is time taken, not rate, so ask yourself what a short time of about 6 minutes at $40 ^\circ\text{C}$ versus about 20 minutes at $20 ^\circ\text{C}$ and $50 ^\circ\text{C}$ really means for speed.

Split the curve into two sections - falling time from $20 ^\circ\text{C}$ to $40 ^\circ\text{C}$ and rising time from $40 ^\circ\text{C}$ to $50 ^\circ\text{C}$ - and recall how warming affects molecular movement and collisions.
Remember respiration is controlled by enzymes, so think about what heat does first to help enzymes meet substrates and then what excess heat does to the shape of the active site.
walkthrough:
Translate time into rate**
The y-axis shows time taken for DCPIP to change colour. A shorter time means faster hydrogen release and faster reduction of DCPIP, so less time = higher respiration rate. Time falls from about 20 minutes at $20 ^\circ\text{C}$ to 10 minutes at $30 ^\circ\text{C}$ to about 6 minutes at $40 ^\circ\text{C}$, then rises sharply to about 21 minutes at $50 ^\circ\text{C}$.

Explain the rise to optimum**
From $20 ^\circ\text{C}$ to $40 ^\circ\text{C}$ rate increases. Higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy, so enzymes and substrates move faster. This gives more frequent successful collisions, more enzyme-substrate complexes formed per unit time, and more enzyme-catalysed respiration reactions.

Explain the fall after optimum**
After $40 ^\circ\text{C}$ rate decreases. Excess heat breaks bonds holding the enzyme in shape, so respiratory enzymes denature and the active site shape changes so substrate no longer fits. $40 ^\circ\text{C}$ is therefore the optimum temperature for yeast respiration in this experiment.

Final answer: Shorter time = higher rate of respiration, ora; rate increases up to $40 ^\circ\text{C}$ due to increased kinetic energy leading to more successful enzyme-substrate collisions and more enzyme-substrate complexes; rate decreases after $40 ^\circ\text{C}$ due to denaturation of respiratory enzymes with change in active site shape; $40 ^\circ\text{C}$ is optimum.
